This study investigates two-layer neural networks, specifically rectified linear unit networks with symmetric weights, trained using a layer-style approach. The analysis focuses on functions defined over the hypercube and demonstrates that, for most network configurations, the generalization error slightly exceeds that of a random network. The findings also show that this random network performance advantage diminishes as the hypercube dimensionality increases. The research relies on a new, established result from random matrix theory, which facilitates the derivation of a new expression for the expected performance of a two-layer neural network.

The Large Hadron Collider's Air Shower Array (LHCAA) is a recently completed experiment designed to study extremely energetic cosmic rays, utilizing their interaction with the LHC's magnetic field. This project aims to study the behavior of cosmic rays with energies ranging from 4 to 32 Exaelectronvolts (EeV) by examining their dipole anisotropy patterns. The results show that the dipole amplitude is 1.5% for 4 EeV cosmic rays and decreases as energy increases, but the dipole amplitude is 3.5% for 32 EeV cosmic rays. The data also reveals that the distribution of cosmic ray arrival directions is not uniform, with the most energetic group exhibiting a significant excess of sources in the direction of the LHC's beam pipe. The results suggest that the most energetic cosmic rays may be influenced by their magnetic environment, with the most likely explanation being that they are deflected by the magnetic field of the LHC's beam pipe.

The concept of geometric almost-periodicity, which has proven useful in analyzing high-dimensional structures, is now being applied to understand the homogenization of thin-dimensional surfaces. This approach yields the first rigorous mathematical foundation for recent 'physicist's' proposals. The resulting mathematical framework provides precise estimates on how quickly the homogenization process converges, which in turn offers a clearer understanding of how quickly this process slows down as the complexity of the underlying pattern increases.

This study examines initial value problems for the Dirac equation set within the framework of a Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robert-Walker (FLRW) spacetime, characterized by either a spatial curvature of zero or a flat metric. We demonstrate that, for power-law scale factors, solutions to the Dirac equation asymptotically behave differently depending on the rate at which they disperse as time progresses, ultimately diverging from standard free solutions. Moreover, we investigate the scenario of exponential scale factors and show that solutions in this case can maintain their asymptotic profile, yet diverge from canonical Dirac framework due to the expanding spacetime.

Cancer immunotherapy has emerged as a groundbreaking treatment, and understanding the cellular composition of tumor microenvironments is crucial for predicting responses to this treatment. The analysis of digitized tissue sections can provide valuable insights into the spatial relationships between tumor cells and immune cells, which are essential for uncovering the underlying mechanisms driving cancer progression and immune responses. The challenge lies in accurately identifying and classifying cell types within these images, which are often obscured by staining and image quality issues. This problem is particularly pressing in cancer research, which demands precise and efficient methods for cell identification and classification. The development of deep learning algorithms has shown promise in addressing this challenge, and this study aims to contribute to this effort by providing a comprehensive dataset of annotated tumor microenvironment images for cell type prediction.

A cutting-edge approach to manipulating quantum systems involves harnessing the interaction between magnons, photons, and phonons within cavity magnomechanics. The advent of two-dimensional magnetic materials has provided a groundbreaking opportunity for exploring new quantum phenomena and achieving precise quantum control. This study pioneers the application of these materials in cavity magnomechanics to facilitate innovative approaches to quantum engineering. By combining a 2D magnetic material with a mechanical resonator and an optical cavity, researchers can leverage the strong coupling between these components to develop advanced protocols for entanglement generation and precise manipulation of quantum states. The unique properties of 2D magnetic materials enable a new class of interactions that were previously unattainable, offering a promising pathway for the development of advanced quantum technologies.

Our framework enables a self-taught, versatile walking system for the ANYmal robot, allowing it to adapt its gait in real-time for complex tasks like climbing steep inclines and navigating uneven surfaces. By using a reinforcement learning approach, the ANYmal's joint angles are adjusted through the modification of a low-dimensional policy, which is trained offline and can be applied to multiple robots without retraining. The framework's efficiency is further enhanced by the incorporation of a simulation-to-real transfer method, which allows the policy to be deployed on a new robot instantly. Our system successfully trains the policy to facilitate real-time walking adaptation and has been applied to challenging climbing tasks, including vertical surface navigation and navigation through narrow obstacles.

The central region of the Milky Way's nucleus is characterized by a Low Mass X-ray Binary system that emits X-rays, which are thought to drive a hot wind. This hot wind is believed to play a crucial role in the galaxy's evolution through feedback mechanisms. To investigate this, we conducted simulations using the ENZO code to model the interaction between the hot wind and the surrounding galaxy. We varied the nuclear scale height and found that the hot wind's expansion is significantly influenced by the nuclear scale height. When the wind is launched from a compact region, it expands rapidly and mixes with the surrounding gas. However, when the wind is launched from a larger region, it expands more slowly and mixes with the surrounding gas less efficiently. Our results suggest that the hot wind's impact on the galaxy's evolution is highly dependent on the region from which it is launched.

In the context of linear quadratic regulation under uncertain disturbances, stochastic reinforcement learning is employed to find the optimal policy for disturbance attenuation. A key challenge in applying reinforcement learning is its slow transient convergence rate. This paper introduces two strategies to address this issue. A novel model-free design technique enhances the learning algorithm's transient performance by leveraging a linear transformation of the disturbance signal. Additionally, a low-pass filter is used to optimize reinforcement learning performance by reducing noise in the data. This is accomplished by adjusting the filter's parameters to balance computational efficiency and convergence stability. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of both proposed methods in improving reinforcement learning's transient convergence.

The SiD calorimeter, a key component of the SiD Detector, is designed to achieve top-tier performance in jet energy resolution within the 30-100 GeV range, primarily for Higgs boson analysis, and also excels in jet energy resolution above 100 GeV, which is crucial for $t\bar t$ mass measurements and $W$ boson analyses.

We conducted a detailed analysis of the metal and abundance composition of Tononzintla 2, a globular cluster candidate in the Milky Way's bulge, using high-resolution spectra from the MIKE spectrograph. Our study of 15 red giant members revealed a metallicity of [Fe/H] = -0.19 +/- 0.05, indicating slightly higher metal content than the Sun. Additionally, we found significant abundance variations in elements such as calcium, titanium, and nickel, with spreads of 0.25 dex, 0.3 dex, and 0.2 dex respectively. These variations are unusually large for a cluster of this metallicity and contradict the expected homogeneity in metal-poor clusters. Our findings suggest that further observations are necessary to confirm Tononzintla 2 as a globular cluster candidate.

Deep learning has significantly advanced remote sensing, yet a comprehensive understanding of its methods' performance in real-world applications is still lacking. To address this knowledge gap, we present EarthNets, a web-based platform that aggregates and standardizes remote sensing datasets and deep learning models for comparison. EarthNets facilitates model evaluation by enabling the integration of diverse datasets and pre-trained models via a unified API. Through the EarthNets platform, we demonstrate the potential for evaluating and disseminating deep learning methods in remote sensing by providing a common framework for model comparison and evaluation.

We've developed a theoretical framework to analyze active nematic systems in two dimensions. This framework enables us to examine orientational order, the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, and topological defects within these systems. This theory is then applied to understand how active stress influences the dynamics of two-dimensional nematics confined to a surface. This specific case is relevant to biological systems, such as epithelial tissues, where nematic order is prevalent. Our results indicate that active stress generates energy fluctuations that increase with wave number, causing the active system to deviate from equilibrium behavior. This non-equilibrium behavior is characterized by a breakdown of the fluctuation-dissipation relation and anisotropic diffusion. This theoretical model is further validated by comparing it to molecular dynamics simulations of active nematic systems.

This research introduces a novel deep learning technique to identify and segment regions of interest in medical imaging, specifically for identifying lung nodules in chest X-rays. The method dynamically divides images into sections to enhance detection of small and irregularly positioned areas. It employs a combination of convolutional neural networks and attention mechanisms to focus on significant areas within each section. The technique's efficiency is maintained by using a U-Net-based network that can be trained end-to-end. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on the public Lung Image Database Consortium (LIDC) dataset, where it outperformed grid-based approaches and achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.724 for nodule detection.

A comprehensive approach to the two-pion effect on the muon anomalous magnetic moment has been developed, focusing on the direct contribution from $I=0$ two-pion states and their connection to scattering data. By utilizing experimental $\pi\pi$ scattering phase shifts and applying a unitary framework, the study quantifies the relevant muon $g-2$ term arising from $\pi\pi$ $I=0$ s-wave interactions. Results indicate a significant influence of the direct two-pion effect, amounting to approximately $-120$ times $10^{-11}$ within the considered energy range. Furthermore, the study extends to resonance contributions from the $\rho$ and the $f_0(980)$, with the latter requiring an additional input due to the absence of its $\pi\pi$ scattering amplitude. By leveraging $\pi K$ scattering data and applying constraints from $\pi\pi$ scattering and isospin symmetry, the study estimates the $f_0(980)$ effect to be around $-13$ times $10^{-11}$. Combined, the scalar sector influence amounts to approximately $-133$ times $10^{-11}$.

Recent breakthroughs in language understanding and generation have significantly
advanced the programming domain, primarily due to the shared complexity between
natural language and code. Recent pre-trained models have shown great potential
in code completion and compilation, learning syntax and semantics from existing
code. This pre-training enables enhanced performance in various programming
applications, including automated code repair. This paper presents a pre-training
method for code repair, leveraging a code representation to predict the specific
location of the error and the necessary changes to fix it. Using the efficient
CodeLMADE model, we demonstrate that our approach effectively completes
corrupted functions, outperforming existing models in over 90% of the
evaluation cases.

The distinct formation processes of galactic discs and bulges versus elliptical galaxies and the galactic halos suggest a segmented approach to understanding galaxy formation. This segmented theory is supported by the separate roles of baryonic processes and dark matter in shaping galaxy structure. The major merger event serves as a key mechanism to explain the segmented formation, with simulations of galaxy interactions revealing how angular momentum is conserved in the resulting discs and halos. The halos, however, are affected by complex feedback processes involving supernovae and active galactic nuclei, which can lead to the expulsion of gas and dark matter. The application of this framework to the Milky Way and M31 reveals that their galactic discs and halos may have developed through distinct processes, with the halos potentially influenced by feedback mechanisms. This segmented approach to understanding galaxy formation is further illustrated by the comparison of the Milky Way and M31 to other galaxy pairs, such as NGC 4485 and M84, which exhibit similar characteristics.

A new approach for calculating the vertical aerosol optical depth is presented, leveraging wide-field photometry to compare the brightness of the same sky region at different times with distinct moon illumination levels. This method does not depend on absolute calibration and can be executed using data from photometric systems that are not precisely calibrated. The technique's effectiveness is demonstrated using the full archival dataset from the Arecibo Lunar Scattering Experiment, resulting in optical depth measurements that align with those obtained through a different method using photometric observations of the moon's limb.

This paper expands the Graphical Lasso framework by incorporating Gaussian latent variables, resulting in a more precise graph representation of observed data. The proposed method combines Graphical Lasso with a latent feature extraction technique to define the precision matrix of observed data in terms of latent variables. Graphical Lasso is then reformulated based on this new definition. Given the intractability of the resulting problem, we develop an alternative approach by reformulating the problem as convex optimization and introducing additional constraints. This enables efficient GLOLLA solver, which can produce both a precise graph of relevant data relationships and a set of underlying latent features.

Our research involves developing a novel disk model that simulates a disk surrounding a star, incorporating three distinct zones: a molecular disk, a dust sublimation layer, and a dust disk. We apply radiative transfer to each area to calculate thermal and X-ray emissions, as well as free-free and free-bound emissions resulting from stellar X-ray irradiation. The X-ray luminosity's impact on the inner disk is significant, resulting in free-free and free-bound emissions that can be as high as the dust emission at certain wavelengths. These emissions originate from ionized gas in the disk's surface layers, which are heated to temperatures between 10,000 and 20,000 K. The free-free and free-bound emissions are particularly noticeable in systems with low dust temperatures, where they can be up to a factor of 10 higher than the disk's total emission.

Our algorithm identifies and eliminates yodeling voices from a dataset by analyzing pitch contours.
We've developed a novel yodeling detection method that pinpoints pitch values unaffected by noise or yodeling, by leveraging an expert system.
Our approach also involves a new yodeling-specific noise type, which results in underestimated pitch values.
To address this, we've designed a pitch contour analysis module to accurately identify yodeling voices.
In our experiments, the system successfully identified yodeling voices in around 80% of cases.
We've also developed an automatic pitch contour modification method to smooth out the speech of identified yodeling voices.
Our modifications resulted in noticeable improvements in the speech of yodeling voices.

The time complexity of solving nonlinear monotone inclusion problems using the DWIFOB algorithm with time-varying dwell times is analyzed. A novel variant of the DWIFOB algorithm, featuring regularization and designed to enhance stability, is also proposed. In comparison to its counterpart, this new method exhibits greater resistance to excessive residence times. Furthermore, the robustness of this modified algorithm surpasses that of the commonly employed Anderson acceleration with regularization. A key property of the algorithm is its ability to achieve linear convergence under suitable conditions, a feature supported by a newly developed nonstationary convexity framework.

This investigation explores the non-minimal supersymmetric standard model (NMSSM) in conjunction with a beyond-standard-model neutrino sector. By incorporating right-handed and left-handed sterile neutrinos, we expand upon existing Higgs and dark matter models to address current neutrino anomalies. Utilizing a Bayesian statistical approach, we analyze how these additional neutrino states influence NMSSM parameter space, particularly in relation to Higgs boson mass predictions and dark matter candidate masses. Our findings indicate that incorporating a neutrino sector significantly widens the Higgs boson mass range consistent with experimental data, and that NMSSM dark matter can span a broader mass spectrum.

Recent breakthroughs in Neural Architecture Search (NAS) have led to a vast number of proposed methods, despite the lack of a comprehensive understanding of their inner workings. Our study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by investigating the relationship between neural architectures and their corresponding programs, employing program property analysis and clustering techniques. We analyzed a substantial dataset comprising 10,000 architectures generated through search using ESBN and PDSBO methods. Our findings indicate that the majority of program properties remain consistent across models with similar validation accuracies, and that the distribution of program properties varies according to validation performance. We also discovered that models with the same program properties exhibit similar structural characteristics, and that the distribution of program properties forms a continuous spectrum rather than distinct clusters. These results offer a new perspective on the field of NAS and provide valuable insights for future research.

This study explores the benefits of using multiple antennas at the receiver in mmWave multicasting systems. To optimize the performance of these systems, we develop a joint design for beamforming and precoding that maximizes a common metric across all users. This is achieved by converting a complex problem into simpler subproblems that can be solved efficiently. The performance of our proposed solution is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate its effectiveness in ensuring consistent data rates for all users.

This study introduces Compressed Federated Distillation, a novel training approach for distributed machine learning that enables knowledge transfer between a server and multiple clients while accounting for limited client storage and reduced communication needs. To address storage constraints, clients maintain a compact model and transmit it to the server, which shares target labels. The server then sends annotated data to the clients, who adjust their models based on this information. To minimize communication costs, the server transmits only a subset of its data to the clients. Theoretical analysis reveals that this approach achieves optimal performance with fewer rounds of interaction and requires less bandwidth per round than traditional Federated Distillation. Furthermore, Compressed Federated Distillation demonstrates improved accuracy compared to Federated Averaging with equivalent communication resources. The algorithm's efficacy is confirmed through experiments on several datasets, including CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.

This study introduces the Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO) algorithm, designed to optimize service delivery in mobile edge computing networks. Unlike current approaches, SDADO considers the challenges of mobile service delivery, such as network latency and service connectivity. It employs a multi-hop discovery approach to locate quality endpoints within a specified access delay. To balance performance and connectivity, the algorithm uses a dynamic orchestration method that prioritizes high-quality and reachable endpoints. Simulation results show SDADO outperforms existing approaches, achieving a 20% improvement in average end-to-end delay, 25% better average throughput, and 30% lower service disruption rates.

We examine the exponential stability of a damped wave equation on a star-shaped metric graph with multiple finite branches and a central measurement point. The damping is pointwise on the central point of the graph. The system's stability is analyzed in the absence of additional factors such as coupling with a heat equation or fractional damping. The primary objective is to investigate whether damping is sufficient for exponential stability on the graph. The system's stability is determined by its eigenvalues, which are analyzed in detail. The results indicate that despite the absence of elasticity on the slopes, the damping is sufficient for exponential stability on the graph.

In a three-flavor NJL model with a linear sigma component, we investigate inhomogeneous chiral phase transitions through a 2+1 dimensional lattice Chiral Random-Phase Approximation. By introducing a constant matter density, we find that the critical temperature for chiral phase transitions decreases. The inhomogeneous condensate exhibits instability in the vector channel rather than the scalar channel. As matter density increases, the transition temperature initially rises before declining. The resulting phase diagram reveals a mixed vector-scalar inhomogeneous phase adjacent to the homogeneous vector phase.

The compound $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ ($M$ = Li, Na, K, or Cs) is an ideal multiferroic material with a tetragonal structure and belongs to the same family as $M$Bi$_4$Te$_3$. It exhibits a high thermoelectric coefficient and can be doped to enhance its electrical conductivity. With its high Curie temperature and ability to be doped, $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ is a suitable candidate for spin torque equipment and spin devices. In this research, we investigated the spin polarization of $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ using first-principles calculations. We found that $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ has a high spin polarization of 0.75, making it a promising material for spintronic applications.

This study diverges from the conventional pairwise optimization of a function by proposing an alternative approach that leverages a utility function to order task outcomes. Unlike past methods that relied on the utility function being implicitly defined through pairwise results, our technique learns a utility function offline using pre-existing expert knowledge. This knowledge can encompass a variety of forms, such as explicit pairwise results, explicit utility functions, or objective criteria. We demonstrate the utility of our method in a real-world task involving offline multi-objective active learning for scientific data labeling. By incorporating a weighting function to incorporate expert knowledge, our approach effectively combines multiple labeling objectives. Furthermore, our results show that utilizing pre-existing expert knowledge significantly enhances the quality of labeling compared to only considering pairwise results.

In the realm of artificial intelligence, sequence-to-sequence models have gained significant attention for their ability to process sequential data. Building on this concept, we introduce a novel approach to predicting the future actions of trained reinforcement learning agents. By treating an existing trained agent as a sequence generator, we can leverage sequence-to-sequence models to outperform traditional methods in this regard. Our study focuses on comparing the efficacy of sequence-to-sequence and recurrent neural networks in predicting the actions of trained reinforcement learning agents across various benchmark environments. Our findings demonstrate that reinforcement learning agents exhibit learnable patterns in their decision-making process, which can be effectively captured and predicted by sequential neural models. Our results also reveal that, in certain complex environments, the sequence-to-sequence model surpasses the reinforcement learning agent itself, thereby offering valuable insights into the decision-making processes of artificial intelligence.

By applying different on-site potentials to the hopping terms in a honeycomb structure, specifically to the nearest, next-nearest and intermediate-hopping connections, the characteristics of the resulting system can be significantly altered. In this study, we investigate a three-dimensional honeycomb lattice with multiple hopping components and demonstrate that it is possible to obtain a type of effective model, such as a three-dimensional herringbone structure, through the application of strong hopping to weaker ones. The effective Hamiltonian of the three-dimensional herringbone structure exhibits a Dirac cone at the Gamma point, and by introducing a hexagonal warping term, it is found that the material's Fermi surface displays a closed, warped circular shape.

Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms that consider risks often produce subpar outcomes when applied to dynamically changing settings. Current solutions that address this issue typically involve algorithms based on dynamic programming, which can be impractical for large-scale problems due to their inability to scale effectively. This paper presents a novel, scalable framework for solving scalable Bellman equations with bounded variability. The proposed framework utilizes restart-based algorithms, which periodically reset the problem and search for new solutions. This approach enables efficient sampling of the problem space and leverages risk-sensitive algorithms that are robust to dynamic changes. Theoretical analysis of the framework is provided, along with empirical evidence demonstrating its effectiveness in simulated environments.

In 2021, Google Open Source Projects initiated the second phase of their Jira project open data release, encompassing a comprehensive dataset of two million public project issues from two thousand projects. This release includes access to project profiles, issue descriptions, comments, attachments, and transition statuses. The projects span public domains, covering areas such as software, hardware, and Android. The data enables a range of analyses, including bug detection, project management, and team collaboration. The projects were sourced from the Atlassian Jira platform, and their release is intended to foster further research into software engineering and open-source development.

In distributed machine learning, we investigate a communication-efficient paradigm where a central server manages multiple clients, each with a subset of the total data. This setup involves two key components: the central server applies a specific aggregation function to receive updates from the clients, and the clients perform local stochastic gradient descent using their local data. We introduce the concept of "weighted power-p m-norm" aggregation, a non-linear method that surpasses linear aggregation, and prove its effectiveness in achieving optimal convergence rates for achieving the best possible outcome on the global problem. We demonstrate that increasing the non-linearity of the aggregation function leads to faster convergence and thus, we establish a theoretical framework for communication-efficient distributed learning.

A new type of single-photon detector has been developed, consisting of a special atom that can be positioned near an optical cavity which in turn is connected to a single-mode fiber. The detector operates by using a specific quantum state of the atom that can be manipulated to create a specific response to the presence of a single photon, resulting in a measurable change in fluorescence emitted from the atom. The proposed method has the potential to be used in various applications, including quantum communication and the study of single atoms and photons in optical systems.

This study investigates valuated oriented graphs where edge weights are determined by a function from an ordered monoid to positive real numbers. We focus on subgraphs resembling 'C' shapes and analyze their properties under a specific partial order. We introduce a method to generate closed sets of words based on a valuated graph, which enable efficient computation of shortest paths without forming cycles. We demonstrate that these closed sets have a straightforward structure and can be represented as the increasing unfolding of'simple' closed sets. We also show that the shortest path between two vertices lies within their shared, closed set of paths. We provide a dynamic programming algorithm for computing these shared sets and use it to develop a method for identifying'shortest' 'C' shaped cycles in the graph.

We've developed a novel approach to identifying polymers using a directed acyclic graph that summarizes the polymer's composition, effectively representing it as a set of monomers and their frequencies. This representation enables us to efficiently calculate key statistical measures, such as mutual information and entropy, which are crucial in understanding the inherent properties of directed acyclic graphs. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the proposed inference method outperforms traditional character-based approaches in classifying polymers and in recognizing the inherent structure of classification data, even in the absence of labeled information.

To effectively treat COVID-19 patients, we need a reliable method to deliver the appropriate amount of air to each patient simultaneously using one ventilator. We've developed a technique to provide each of four patients with the required lung volume over a 12-second cycle using a dual-valve system. Our approach involves synchronizing the lung delivery to each patient's unique breathing pattern by timing the valve openings. We've validated the method through numerical simulations and tested it using a physical setup.

We've established that the deck transformation groups resulting from iterating bicritical rational maps have a specific structure, which we've also used to identify these iterations with positive degree as normal subgroups within the total monodromy group. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the external degree of these maps remains constant across all iterations beyond a certain point.

In a standard Bayesian linear regression model with an unknown error variance, considering a Gibbs prior on the regression coefficient and an inverse gamma prior on the variance, research has shown that the posterior distribution converges at specific rates under certain conditions. However, recent findings contradict these results, demonstrating that taking the unknown error variance into account significantly affects posterior contraction rates. Through direct Bayesian analysis, it has been proven that the joint distribution of the error variance and regression coefficient posterior distributions converges at specific rates under different scenarios, while the marginal distribution of the regression coefficient posterior distribution converges at different rates compared to known error variance scenarios. The inverse gamma prior is the primary focus of this research, but the results can be extended to other prior distributions, such as the half-student t prior.

A novel machine learning framework has been developed to predict surface roughness in machining processes, with an emphasis on understanding the interplay between machining parameters and outcomes. Various regression algorithms were tested to predict surface roughness, with the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM) model emerging as the most effective. Analysis using LGBM revealed that the feed rate has the most significant impact on surface roughness, followed by cutting speed and tool wear. Feature importance assessment using LGBM, correlation analysis, and mutual information all confirmed the feed rate's dominant influence. The LGBM's superior performance over other regression models, including Random Forest and Support Vector Regression, further validated its efficacy in capturing the complex relationships between machining parameters and surface roughness.

We establish a linear relationship between specific distorted metric spaces derived from the Dirichlet energy of metric spaces and metric spaces with controlled distortion. These spaces are defined based on the optimal smooth structures and structures with bounded weighted Poincaré inequalities, respectively. The first inequality provides a lower bound for the Dirichlet energy of a map from a metric space with controlled distortion to a metric tree, while the second offers an upper bound for the Dirichlet energy of a weighted map from a metric space with controlled distortion to a metric tree. The tree maps considered have constant images on connected components. The results imply that the set of distances with controlled distortion from a metric space has at most one element up to scaling, while the set of images with optimal tree representation from a metric space has at most one element up to scaling.

We explore the implications of mixing between bottomonium states in the 
$\eta_{\unicode{x2019}}(1S)$-$\eta_{b}(2S)$ system on hadronic properties. 
Our analysis employs the hadronic transition amplitudes for 
$\eta_{\unicode{x2019}}(1S)$-$\eta_{b}(1S)$ and 
$\eta_{\unicode{x2019}}(2S)$-$\eta_{b}(1S)$, which are derived from 
lattice QCD calculations. We utilize these calculations to obtain the 
$\theta$-$\theta'$ mixing angle and investigate its impact on hadronic 
properties, including the decay rates of $\eta_{b}(2S)$ and 
$\eta_{\unicode{x2019}}(2S)$. Additionally, we examine the radiative 
decays of $\eta_{b}(2S)$ and $\eta_{\unicode{x2019}}(2S)$ into 
$\psi(\unicode{x2019})P$ and $\psi(P)$-$f_{0}(980)$, 
respectively, where $P$ represents a light pseudoscalar meson. 
The results of our study indicate that $\theta$-$\theta'$ mixing may be 
detectable in future experiments and provide valuable insights into 
hadronic properties.

The growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to a surge in connected devices, which has also made them vulnerable to cyber threats. To address this concern, a novel approach has been developed that leverages the inherent biometric properties of devices to ensure their secure communication. In line with this, a signature-based authentication system is proposed, which employs a combination of device fingerprinting and lightweight cryptography to verify the identity of devices during their interactions. To enhance the performance of this system, a set of novel metrics has been devised to evaluate the individual device signature characteristics, ultimately facilitating improved forgery detection capabilities.

We investigate the constraints imposed by supersymmetry on low-energy effective couplings within various string theories, particularly in the context of orientifold models that approach realistic particle physics. The suppositions made about the supersymmetry of the vacuum state enable us to establish precise relationships between the effective field theory parameters. The analysis is carried out for closed and semi-realistic string configurations, with the latter incorporating D-planes. The findings indicate that supersymmetry constraints can be leveraged to further limit the parameter space of low-energy effective couplings, thus narrowing down the possible string theory landscape.

A significant challenge in quantum technology is the impact of thermal noise on the operation of qubits and quantum sensors. This problem is even more pronounced in complex quantum systems that exhibit correlations beyond pairwise interactions. This research investigates how thermal fluctuations affect the existence of intrinsic quantum correlations in many-body systems. We demonstrate that thermal fluctuations have a substantial impact on higher-order correlations, which can emerge even when lower-order thermal noise is minimal. This phenomenon is investigated using a Bose-Hubbard model and the quantum Ising chain. We also examine the thermal behavior of a photonic system exhibiting intrinsic correlations through measurements of photon correlations.

We've developed a new model of galactic chemical evolution that's based on observations of stars in the Milky Way's bulge. The model shows that the rate of star formation in the galaxy has slowed down over time, and that the amount of stars formed at different times has a direct impact on how elements are created and spread throughout the galaxy. The model also reveals that the ratio of nitrogen to oxygen in the galaxy has increased more rapidly than previously thought, and that this is due to nitrogen being produced by a different type of star than oxygen. The findings of our study have significant implications for our understanding of how galaxies form and evolve over time.

This report provides an overview of NLP research and its practical benefits to multilingual communities, highlighting the skills and knowledge required for aspiring researchers. It covers prominent research fields, their significance, and potential career paths within the industry.

The analysis of complex biological systems like the human immune system requires advanced mathematical frameworks that can incorporate networked data and geometric and topological properties. This paper presents a novel approach to analyzing biological systems by combining graph theory, differential geometry, and the analysis of topological properties. Our method involves extracting meaningful features from biological data, such as gene expression profiles, and mapping them onto mathematical structures to identify key characteristics. This approach is demonstrated through a practical application in the analysis of multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer, where we use the analysis of gene expression and the relationships between patient samples to identify disease subtypes and predict outcomes.

We're investigating the production of hidden sector particles within the core of cooling stars, specifically those of the DA type, and cooling faster than expected. Our focus is on the Left-Right Symmetric Model's (LRSM) self-conjugate bi-doublet ($\Delta$) and its associated decay products, which we're analyzing in the context of star cooling rates. The LRsm is characterized by the breaking of its $SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_R \times U(1)_{XY}$ gauge symmetry, initiated by the VEV of the bi-doublet. Our study involves calculating the production rates of $\Delta$ particles via Higgs and triplet boson interactions, as well as their subsequent decay into neutrinos and other particles, in order to establish constraints on the LRSM's parameter space. The constraints are primarily imposed by the observed cooling rates of neutrinos in white dwarfs, specifically those in the globular cluster of the star Sirius. The constraints are further refined by considering the potential impact of $\Delta$-mediated neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu2\nu$) on neutrino oscillation experiments. Our analysis reveals that the LRsm parameter space is largely excluded by existing white dwarf cooling data, and that the neutrinoless double beta decay constraints are insufficient to further limit the model's parameters.

This paper presents an innovative approach to classifying images privately, centered on graph models. We've developed the Graph Privacy Advisor, a graph model that can identify private images within a class, and we've compared it to baseline models. The results show that the Graph Privacy Advisor outperforms these baselines, particularly in cases where training data is limited. Furthermore, we've found that the Graph Privacy Advisor excels at detecting private samples from classes it wasn't trained on. We've also found that the Graph Privacy Advisor is more robust to adversarial attacks than other private classifiers.

Recent research has led to a novel understanding of how entropy flows in systems governed by quantum statistical laws.  The conventional view of the Fock model suggests that only specific types of particles, known as bosons, can exhibit entropy flow due to entanglement.  However, we challenge this perspective by showing that non-classical effects in fermionic and photonic systems also influence entropy flow.  Our study reveals that entropy flow in all four models - Fock, Gibbs, Pauli, and Bose-Einstein - is governed by a unified mathematical framework.  The entropy flow in the latter three models can be expressed as a deviation from the von Neumann law, with this deviation arising from entanglement between different modes of the quantum field.  The model of photons obeying Pauli exclusion principles yields the most substantial entanglement-driven entropy flow.  The entropy flow in systems governed by Pauli statistics exceeds that of bosons, fermions, and photons in the Fock model by a factor of 1.5.

Measurements of photon-tagged jets and inclusive jets in Pb+Pb collisions were conducted using the CMS detector at the LHC. Specifically, jet-photon transverse momentum imbalance was measured for a high-pT photon tag in both Pb+Pb and pp collisions. Additionally, the ratio of Pb+Pb to pp collisions was measured for inclusive jets, and these comparisons were made across different centrality ranges. The observed modifications of photon-tagged jets were significantly greater than those of inclusive jets, and this effect was more pronounced for lower-momentum jets. The results indicate that energy loss mechanisms in these collisions are dependent on the initial and final state of the jet.

The advancement of specialized low-precision hardware has sparked interest in developing efficient algorithms that can utilize lower precision data types. This interest has led to the development of novel computational methods capable of harnessing the potential of such hardware. This survey provides an overview of the techniques employed in scientific computing to lower numerical precision without compromising accuracy, focusing on approaches such as approximate arithmetic, reduced precision data storage, and hardware-specific optimizations. We also examine the performance of these techniques in standalone form and in combination, highlighting key findings and future research directions.

FOXSI's balloon-borne imaging spectrometer has the ability to detect hard X-rays emitted from the quiet Sun, but its capability is hindered by high background noise resulting from cosmic rays and residual gas interactions. To overcome this limitation, FOXSI's data analysis technique utilizes the spatial and spectral information in its data to distinguish between the quiet Sun and background signals. By employing a Bayesian deconvolution approach, researchers can recover the true X-ray spectrum of the quiet Sun, effectively separating it from background signals. When applied to FOXSI's data, this technique reveals the quiet Sun's X-ray spectrum to be consistent with previous observations, but with a higher level of detail and clarity.

Predicting a user's impact within their social network is crucial for various applications, including identifying influential individuals and enhancing online advertising. While traditional methods have been explored, they often struggle with large networks and sparse connections. To address these limitations, we investigated the potential of augmenting graph data during both training and testing phases. Our experiments reveal that augmenting smaller graphs tends to be more effective than larger ones. Furthermore, we found that augmentations applied at test time can complement those used in training, enhancing overall performance.

This study employs a geometric optimization framework to investigate Euler-Arnold equations, which, when applied to certain fields like SU(N) Yang-Mills and SU(N) gravity, can be used to find the most compact configurations of these fields in specific boundary conditions. By employing this framework, we successfully identify the optimal configurations for both fields, which minimize their energy to nearly zero, with the resulting configurations exhibiting properties of zero modes and solitons.

This research focuses on positing a more sophisticated error model for sensor measurements, which incorporates general correlations without being specific to particular measurements. By integrating this model into the estimation process, we can enhance accuracy without needing to know the exact nature of the error correlations. This model, which is based on a nonparametric framework, is then applied to the problem of determining a camera's position using a limited number of feature points. To validate this approach, we conducted experiments using a simulated stereo camera setup, which revealed that considering broader error correlations significantly boosts accuracy when using 100 or fewer feature points.

The concept of a multi-temperature universe is employed to examine the interaction of dark matter particles at different energy levels. This approach is particularly useful for analyzing the performance of dark matter detection methods across various scales and distances. Within this framework, the phase space of dark matter is divided into distinct thermal components, each characterized by its own temperature. This concept is applied to investigate the behavior of dark matter across various scales, such as the galactic, solar, and terrestrial levels. It is demonstrated that a single-temperature model is insufficient to explain the observations, and a more complex two-temperature distribution is required. This is consistent with the findings of recent research on the galactic dark matter profile. Furthermore, a two-temperature model is used to analyze the solar and terrestrial distribution of dark matter, and its implications for direct and indirect detection methods are explored. This approach also provides a more accurate description of the local dark matter density, and its relationship with the local velocity distribution is examined.

An investigation into the production of two W bosons with the same electric charge has been carried out using a dataset of proton-proton collisions collected by the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis, based on data corresponding to 36 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity, focused on events with high transverse momentum W boson decays into leptons and high-energy jet activity. The study found that the number of observed events exceeded standard model predictions by 2.2 standard deviations, with notable increases in predictions seen in specific regions of phase space characterized by large di-lepton invariant mass.

We introduce a novel approach to colorization that combines the efficiency of
pixel-level techniques with the conceptually straightforward and interpretable
method of optimization. The proposed method formulates the colorization task as
finding the optimal color image that minimizes the difference from the given
grayscale image and adheres to semantic color constraints. To achieve this, we
employ a neural network that efficiently predicts color boundaries, enabling us
to quickly converge to a satisfactory solution. The results demonstrate that our
approach surpasses previous methods in color consistency and computational
speed, while also offering an unprecedented level of flexibility in applying
color constraints.

We investigate the cosmological parameters of a closed universe model based on Planck's P(q) data, and compare it to a modified, open universe version of the same data, with a fixed angular scale of acoustic peaks and no spatial flatness. By analyzing the closed universe model with a luminosity distance of 3010 Mpc/h at z=1100 and a new, relaxed distance constraint, we find that the former yields a significantly higher dark energy density and lower matter density than the standard LambdaCDM model. In contrast, the relaxed model produces results that converge towards LambdaCDM. Our study supports the conclusion that Planck's P(q) data alone cannot rule out a closed universe model, especially when combined with other datasets, such as the Planck 2018 results with H0LiCOW's H0 constraint, which yield a closed universe likelihood that is 10 times more probable than a flat universe.

This study examines the maintenance of shared resources in co-located collaborative settings, focusing on the maintenance of shared code in computer science. We investigate the maintenance of shared files in GitHub, revealing significant disparities in maintenance practices between project repositories. Some projects actively maintain shared files, while others neglect them. We identify key characteristics that differentiate well-maintained shared files from poorly maintained ones. Notably, projects with a dedicated team, clear governance structure, and established contribution guidelines are more likely to maintain shared files effectively. We also discuss the implications of these findings and offer suggestions for enhancing the maintenance of shared resources.

Our study of the BD And binary system, which appears to be close to the threshold for nova outbursts, has involved detailed photometric and spectroscopic observations spanning 10 years.  These observations have led us to conclude that BD And is likely an overstripping symbiotic star with a massive white dwarf.  To better understand the system, we have developed a 3D radiative transfer model that accounts for the complex interaction between the cool stellar wind from the red giant and the hot star.  This model has helped us to resolve the observed light curve and spectral features, including the broad Balmer lines and the P Cygni profiles.  However, there are discrepancies between our model and the observed spectra, which may be attributed to the presence of an additional component in the system.  Further observations are necessary to verify this hypothesis.  Additionally, our analysis has provided a more accurate estimate of the system's orbital period, which has implications for understanding the evolution of BD And and its potential future outbursts.

This research demonstrates that the Yamabe flow typically exhibits a unique long-term shape for any given initial shrinking shape. However, we've discovered examples of shrinking shapes that don't settle into a steady state, contrary to existing theories. By developing a new approach, we've proven the existence of both smooth and rough shrinking shapes that don't settle into a steady state, even on manifolds with symmetries.

A novel approach, Preference Learning with Aspect Preference Enhancement (PLAPE), is proposed to enhance the accuracy of recommendation systems by capturing user preferences more precisely. The method employs a novel GAPE module to capture and integrate aspect preferences from multiple user feedback sources, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of users' preferences. The aspect preferences are learned through a contrastive learning framework, and PLAPE's performance is evaluated on real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to outperform existing preference learning models.

This research applies obstruction theory to construct symplectic sheaves from closed differential forms representing specific classes in hypercohomology spaces of Lie algebras. A parallel approach is used to prove the existence of certain symplectic manifolds in foliated spaces under condition (A).

This discussion leverages the power of partition-generating functions to
examine properties of partitions with constraints on part frequency. It
also employs this method to analyze two specific partitions: those of n using
only odd parts and those of n with distinct parts. Furthermore, a linking
relationship between odd and distinct parts is explored.

We investigate the effectiveness of the weighted least-squares method in approximating smooth functions under a given weight, using only exact samples without noise. By strategically choosing weights, we demonstrate that this method ensures optimal stability and convergence rates, thereby providing efficient sample complexity. Furthermore, under the assumption of smoothness, we prove the existence of weights that yield efficient approximations. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments, which illustrate the method's performance in practice.

Using a quarkonium decay model, we investigate the hadronic interaction of the $J/\psi$ with the X(3872) particle, considering two distinct internal structures of X(3872): a tetraquark state and a loosely bound $D\bar D^*$ molecular state. Our analysis reveals that the reaction rates and initial conditions of the $J/\psi$-X(3872) interactions are significantly influenced by the internal structure of X(3872). Furthermore, we find that the $J/\psi$-X(3872) reaction rates can be used to differentiate between the two proposed internal structures of X(3872).

In disordered silicon doped with phosphorus, an experiment has been conducted to study the magnetic properties of the dopant atoms. A specific method was used to create magnetic interactions between the atoms through spin-dependent connections, resulting in a complex many-body system. This system exhibits characteristics of a specific type of magnetic ordering known as the spiral ordered state. This phenomenon is analogous to similar observations in carbon-based materials with interlayer interactions.

The standard combinatorial objects associated with the finite classical Coxeter group B_n are examined in light of the in-depth analysis of its exchange relations based on Coxeter length, descent set, and inversion system. The study focuses on understanding the connections between these parameters and the properties of these combinatorial objects. The research also highlights the implications of these results on understanding Eulerian polynomials and identifying descent classes within the group B_n.

We're investigating a scalar field theory in one spatial dimension with a global U(1) symmetry. The theory includes a real scalar field coupled to a U(1) gauge field through a Higgs portal, as well as an explicit U(1)-breaking complex scalar field. Our calculations show that even with the presence of explicit symmetry breaking, the conserved U(1) current maintains its conservation law. Furthermore, we find that in the absence of explicit symmetry breaking, the conserved U(1) current has non-trivial implications.

This research introduces a novel hierarchical Bayesian model for robot learning in real-world settings, addressing the challenge of a vast number of confounding elements that impact robot performance. By segmenting a robot's learning process into two distinct phases - a high-level phase focused on identifying essential environmental features and a low-level robot learning phase - the model effectively mitigates the effects of confounding variables. A case study involving a robot learning to navigate a room with moving objects demonstrates the model's efficiency in robot learning.

The whisker topology $\tau_w$ and the lasso topology $\tau_l$ are two topological structures that can be applied to the hypertree space $\tilde{X}_{H}$ associated with a hypergraph $H$. The whisker topology is inherently a subset of the lasso topology. The relationship between these two topological structures is such that they are equivalent when the underlying hypergraph $H$ is tripod-free.

In recent years, deep reinforcement learning has made significant advancements in complex, real-world applications. However, a key limitation persists: the motion planning process is typically bypassed in favor of direct action generation, resulting in a lack of explicit consideration for potential future movements. This article proposes an innovative motion planning framework that integrates future movement analysis into the planning process. Our approach leverages a pre-trained neural network to predict potential future movements and their associated rewards, which are then utilized in a planner to determine optimal action sequences. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, showcasing its ability to generate action sequences that are both efficient and adaptable to changing environments.

Our research investigates the long-term growth of supermassive black holes through Eddington-type gas disk accretion. We derived a novel formula for the accreted mass in a disk, which is proportional to the initial gas mass and depends on the ratio of Eddington luminosity to actual luminosity, as well as a time scale related to the disk's mass. We applied this equation to model the growth of central black holes in galaxies, assuming a constant ratio of Eddington luminosity to actual luminosity. We found that for typical star formation rates and Eddington luminosities, the mass accreted over 100 million years is only a small fraction of the mass required for observed black hole mass growth. This suggests that black holes likely experienced periods of higher luminosity and faster accretion during their early growth stages.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various machine learning tasks, particularly in image classification. However, these models often lack interpretability, making it difficult to understand their decision-making process. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages uncertainty quantification to develop more trustworthy and reliable deep learning models. By incorporating an ensemble of deep learning models, we can estimate uncertainties at both the data and predictive output levels. This approach enables us to identify challenging samples that the models struggle to classify, thereby improving overall accuracy. Furthermore, we apply a Bayesian neural network to estimate uncertainties, and evaluate the effectiveness of our method on multiple datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. Our results demonstrate that our approach leads to better accuracy and more reliable uncertainty estimates, ultimately providing a stronger foundation for developing interpretable and trustworthy deep learning models.

This study examines the dissemination of scientific knowledge through preprints, which are early-stage versions of research articles shared freely online. By analyzing over 1,000 physics articles from the 1990s to 2020, we found that preprints significantly accelerate the sharing of new findings, particularly in experimental research. Furthermore, preprints often lead to higher citation rates, which can be attributed to the increased accessibility of the associated research. Notably, this trend is more pronounced in experimental research compared to theoretical research.

This paper outlines our experience in developing and implementing an automated data management system within a laboratory environment. The project's primary objective was to streamline data handling and reduce complexity, particularly in connection with UV-Vis spectroscopy. By integrating the system with instrumental software, it is now possible to automatically populate patient information and sample identifiers across multiple data formats, including electronic records, physical labels, and sample collection tubes. Additionally, the system's features enable the automatic population of sample metadata and the implementation of batch processing capabilities. The system's implementation has resulted in significant improvements to laboratory documentation accuracy and efficiency, and we anticipate that similar benefits can be achieved through customized solutions in other laboratories.

Advanced manufacturing processes have significantly expanded the range of achievable materials, yet the complexity of their microstructures and properties remains a major challenge. To address this, researchers have developed computational methods, such as thermodynamic calculations and molecular dynamics simulations, to guide the design of new materials. However, these techniques are often time-consuming and require significant computational resources. In contrast, machine learning has emerged as a more efficient tool for predicting phase formations, mechanical properties, and optimizing microstructures based on processing parameters. This review provides an overview of the latest progress in data-driven design and processing of advanced materials, highlighting both the potential applications and the remaining challenges.

The decay of the $T_{cc}^{+\tau}$ into $D^+\Sigma^+$ and $D^0\Sigma^+$ is examined with a focus on the effects of $D^{+\tau}D$ and $D^0\Sigma^+$ final state interactions. Utilizing a phenomenological Lagrangian approach, we determine that short-range interactions contribute negligibly to the process. In contrast, long-range interactions mediated by $W$-exchange and light hadron exchanges are dominant, with $D^{+\tau}D$ final state interactions being more pronounced than those of $D^0\Sigma^+$.

Recent advances in Graph Neural Networks have led to significant applications in sub-space learning.  However, the theoretical underpinnings of these methods have been understudied.  This work aims to bridge this knowledge gap by providing a comprehensive analysis of how Graph Neural Networks can be utilized for effective sub-space learning.  The proposed framework leverages the characteristics of data manifolds and the propagation of signals through the graph to achieve optimal sub-space representation.  The theoretical results are substantiated through experiments conducted on image classification and gene expression analysis tasks.

This study delves into the completeness problem of classical Sidon sets in the context of the finite affine plane. We establish a correspondence between hyperbolas and ellipses within this plane and Sidon sets of type I and II respectively. We derive a method to generate all possible ellipses in the plane, and use it to create a comprehensive list of all type II Sidon sets in the affine plane. We also explore the connection between this classification and curves in algebraic geometry, and provide an example of a curve containing points arranged in a specific numerical pattern that does not originate from the same field.

A new method has been developed to efficiently estimate the rank of a binary matrix by sampling rows and columns according to a non-uniform probability distribution. This distribution is based on the fraction of 1s in each row and column, and it has been shown to be more effective than uniform sampling, particularly in cases where the 1s are clustered together. The algorithm leverages this sampling technique to reduce the matrix size, and it is guaranteed to be non-destructive, meaning that each sampled element is independent of the previous ones. The performance of the algorithm is analyzed, and it is demonstrated that it can achieve a significant speedup over uniform sampling, with the non-destructive variant achieving nearly optimal results.

The problem of determining parton distribution functions (PDFs) is a crucial aspect of particle physics, as it involves finding a set of functions that accurately describe the probability of a hadron splitting into a specific parton at a given momentum transfer scale. This problem is essentially a constrained inverse problem, as it is subject to multiple constraints imposed by experimental data and theoretical principles such as DGLAP evolution, parton number conservation, and parton distribution symmetry. To address this issue, we have developed a novel Bayesian framework for fitting PDFs that utilizes regularization to ensure the stability of the solution and incorporates both experimental data and theoretical constraints into a unified likelihood function. This approach allows us to obtain a set of PDFs that are consistent with available data, taking into account measurement uncertainties and correlations. To illustrate the effectiveness of our method, we have applied it to a simplified case of photon PDFs and obtained a set of distributions that are consistent with experimental data, taking into account DGLAP evolution and other relevant constraints.

This article outlines the features and capabilities of the open-source data mining and machine learning toolkit, ELKI, which is designed to support various tasks through multiple algorithms. To enhance its functionality and scalability, the system is built on a modular architecture that allows for parallel processing, significantly improving performance. Additionally, the article highlights additional tools included in ELKI to facilitate data analysis and preprocessing.

We've developed a method to map the spectrum of a tiny microresonator comb by modulating a microdisk with two additional frequency inputs, resulting in a modulated Kerr comb with specific characteristics. Our approach allows for precise identification of individual comb lines, and we've demonstrated this by creating a microcomb with multiple peaks separated by an additional frequency, while also achieving narrow line widths in the microcomb.

We establish that in any torsion-free locally indicable group, a randomly chosen subgroup generated by elements of the group serves as a distinct, inherent subset with specific attributes. This random subset exhibits both faithfulness and weak mixingness. Furthermore, using this finding, a proof is provided showing that in an abelian group with countably many generators, a specific element's power has positive overlap with a randomly chosen element of the group.

We introduce a new class of neural networks called quasi neural networks, which have a parameter that controls the balance between a parameterized component and a fixed component. The fixed component's influence is captured in the neural tangent kernel, while the parameterized component's effect is described by a specific differential equation. The eigenvalue of the neural tangent kernel dictates the fixed component's decay rate, effectively limiting its impact as the network size grows. Consequently, the fixed component behaves similarly to the solution of the differential equation in this asymptotic regime.

The entropic characteristics of holographic CFT states are examined through the lens of entropy, revealing how properties of bulk entropies influence those of boundary entropies. It is observed that bulk entanglement features, such as the entanglement of formation and residual entanglement, are reflected in the corresponding boundary entropies. Furthermore, the entropic behavior of bulk states is found to be consistent with the requirements of quantum mechanics, specifically the constraints imposed by the laws of thermodynamics and the unitary nature of the system. The imposition of the monogamy of mutual information for bulk entropies has significant implications for boundary entropies, leading to the conclusion that bulk entropy satisfies strong subadditivity. The analysis also investigates how boundary entropies respond to the introduction of additional regions and how this affects the entanglement structure of the system.

A novel probabilistic framework is developed to analyze the integrable SOS and RSOS models. The local state probabilities are represented using the polynomial definition of the SOS/RSOS models, expressed as a sum over the weight functions of semi-standard Young tableaux. By applying the branching rule, state probabilities can be written using standard Young tableaux, facilitating asymptotic analysis. The developed framework is adaptable to various boundary conditions, including diagonal, horizontal, and vertical stratifications.

We investigate the one-step recovery of a sparse signal from underdetermined linear measurements, focusing on the impact of combining various stabilization techniques on performance and robustness. By integrating procedures such as the Euclidean projection onto the $\ell_1$-ball, truncation, and clipping, we demonstrate that the $\ell_1$-projection's inclusion is essential for achieving optimal results, whereas the simultaneous application of all three yields the most robust outcome. Our analysis, which employs a fixed point approach, reveals that the $\ell_1$-projection's incorporation enables optimal convergence rates, whereas its absence leads to suboptimal performance, albeit with improved stability in certain cases.

We assess the effectiveness of four different algorithms for combining astronomical images in preserving star and galaxy shapes. These algorithms include simple averaging, averaging with outliers removed, taking the middle value, and averaging with outliers removed in a Jackknife method. Images from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys are used to test these algorithms. Our findings indicate that the averaging algorithm with outliers removal and the Jackknife method successfully combine images without distorting stellar morphology, whereas the median algorithm fails to do so. These combining algorithms also have varying impacts on measured galaxy elongation, with the averaging algorithm with outliers removal and the Jackknife method introducing a slight bias towards more elongated shapes, while the median algorithm introduces a bias towards more elongated shapes in the opposite direction. These findings have implications for cosmological measurements that rely on galaxy elongation as a proxy for redshift.

This study introduces an expansion of Schramm–Loewner evolution (SLE) to a chordal context, incorporating an imaginary surface element that's invariant under SLE growth and breakdown. An invariance theorem is formulated and proven, which also yields a novel integral representation for imaginary SLE. We establish a connection between imaginary SLE and the imaginary geometric SLE defined in prior research, as well as an interpretation of imaginary SLE in terms of a conformally invariant point process on a complex plane.

For the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with periodic boundary conditions, we consider a scenario where the initial velocity field has zero mean and is periodic across all axes. We have developed a solution method that allows us to prove, under certain conditions, that there exists a unique local-in-time smooth solution to these equations. Notably, our approach does not require the initial data to be divergence-free. We have also obtained a key property of this solution, showing that the maximum norm of its derivative components is bounded by the maximum norm of the initial data, scaled by a specific time-dependent factor.

A revolutionary CNOT verification scheme has been devised, allowing for the verification of multi-qubit circuits using a single qubit input in a parallel process. In contrast to serial verification methods, this innovative protocol can efficiently verify n-qubit circuits with only $\log_2 n$ input qubits. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the new protocol maintains a verification success rate of at least 99.24% for all circuits n qubits in size, and it has been found to enhance verification speeds by a factor of up to 100 times in the most extensive case tested.

A novel approach to creating realistic cell shapes using deep generative models is presented, which has significant potential applications in biomedical image analysis. By enhancing existing image datasets with synthetic cell masks, these models can improve the accuracy of critical tasks like tracking and cell segmentation. We propose a new method for generating high-quality, diverse cell shapes that accurately capture the complexity of real biological cells. This method employs a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN) to create mask images conditioned on outer cell boundary images, which are in turn generated by an unconditional generator. We evaluate our model on a large dataset consisting of 10,000 cell masks extracted from time-lapse microscopy videos of amoeba-like cells. The model successfully produces high-quality, diverse cell shapes, which can be used to augment existing datasets for cell tracking and segmentation analysis.

Reinforcement learning agents in simple visual environments have been observed to create internal representations that preserve external features over time. Although this behavior has been seen in multiple studies, its functional significance remains unclear. A new investigation explores how maintaining external features internally affects task performance in geometric problems. Agents were trained to complete either straightforward linear tasks or more complex branched environments, either with or without pressure to maintain features. Analysis of the internal representations showed that pressure to maintain features led to the creation of temporal internal structures, regardless of the task complexity. Interestingly, only in the branched environment setting did maintaining features translate to improved task performance. This highlights the importance of understanding internal neural network behaviors and their functional implications.

We introduce a computational method for simulating classical many-body systems with a long-range, non-local force that acts in addition to a short-range interaction. The main force considered is a magnetic dipole-dipole interaction, but the method can also be used for other types of forces. The method is based on an extension of the McCloy-Cash-Dynard equation of motion cell-based Monte Carlo algorithm. The original MCECM was introduced in a study on two-dimensional dipolar systems, and we adapt it for simulating three-dimensional models. However, we find that it suffers from dynamical arrest due to very long relaxation times. To address this issue, we develop a Newtonian variant of the MCECM that successfully overcomes the problem of stagnation. The computational efficiency of the new method is demonstrated by showing that it can simulate a three-dimensional system of 10,000 particles with a global relaxation time of 100 iterations.

This research investigates the effectiveness of various data augmentation techniques in enhancing sound event detection performance. We examine how different methods, including spectral augmentation and synthetic sound generation, affect the L-AMBR metric across multiple datasets. Notably, we found that spectral augmentation methods, such as Spectral augmentation and Filterbank pruning, have a limited impact on the L-AMBR metric. Conversely, using synthetic sounds for augmentation showed considerable improvement in the L-AMBR metric, particularly when applied to the ESC-50 dataset.

A linear multiple access channel model is examined, focusing on how a single antenna decodes multiple users' messages in a layered approach. We establish a mathematical framework for superposition properties in multiple access channels, revealing how layered data separation in the code domain differs from traditional layered data separation in the frequency domain. We demonstrate superposition additivity and additivity additivity in specific scenarios, and how these distinctions impact real-world applications like federated learning and non-orthogonal multiple access. We also explore how layered multiple access channels can be trained and how this affects user data rate and learning efficiency.

A novel approach to signal detection and estimation in the spectrogram is developed, utilizing level sets to represent frequency-time regions where signal power exceeds a certain threshold. This method enables the estimation of signal parameters, such as onset time and end time, by optimizing level set parameters. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful detection of bird songs and musical notes.

We introduce a straightforward method for identifying synchronized clusters in complex systems, determining both their count and the level of synchronization within each. Our approach involves using a measure of synchronization and an optimization technique to identify the most synchronized states in the system's configuration space. We validate our technique on various models, including a network of coupled oscillators with random frequencies and a brain activity dataset, comparing the results to traditional methods of analyzing synchronization.

A novel machine learning module has been developed to simulate complex physical systems involving moving particles and fluid dynamics. Built upon a foundation of geometric representation, this module uses a frame-based approach to track the state of a system, providing translation and rotation invariance. It has been applied to model oscillating pendulums, gravitational demonstrations, and objects interacting with fluids, offering advantages of grid-free simulation and compatibility with rotated and shifted initial conditions.

This study presents an innovative method for creating quantum information engines through the use of stochastic quantum jump measurements.  Unlike conventional measurement approaches, our proposal incorporates a continuous measurement process, enabling the extraction of information on a continuous timescale.  By utilizing a specific type of entangled state known as a W state, the system exhibits measurable differences in its efficiency, which become more pronounced as the scale of the system increases.  The results of our analysis indicate that quantum effects can significantly enhance the performance of these engines, and that their performance can be optimized by adjusting the level of dissipation in the system.

In a study of the Archimedes Poultry problem, we investigated how a two-dimensional disk pile behaves within a confined square container. We varied the disk weights, assigning them randomly, and analyzed the piles that formed. Our simulation revealed that the arrangement of the disk piles was dependent on their weight distribution. We found that the critical parameter determining the disk pile's structure was the ratio of the heaviest to lightest disk weights. We observed that when this parameter was below a critical threshold, the disk pile would adopt a particular configuration, whereas above this point, the disk pile would assume a different, more complex structure. We also discovered that the density of the disk piles, as well as the number of disk piles that formed, were both dependent on this critical parameter.

Research has shown that certain weather patterns linked to El Niño and La Niña can be reliably predicted months in advance. However, recent studies have discovered that not all variations of El Niño and La Niña exhibit the same characteristics.
